author: Autodesk
description: MPM rubber scene that shows surfacing workflow
documentation:
## Rubber Helix Graph

### Description

This graph shows how to use the MPM solver to simulate two interlocking rubber helices.

The MPM rubber material is a simpler material than snow, sand or gel, with purely elastic behavior. This means the performance is faster as well. If you were to change the material to be sand with a large amount of friction and cohesion, the material behavior would be very similar however the performance wouldn't be as fast. In the Maya profiler the event `Simulation::MPM::Internal::Rubber::momentum_update` shows how much time is used simulating the specifically the rubber, similarly the event `Simulation::MPM::Internal::Sand::momentum_update` would show the time used for sand.  The other `Simulation::MPM` event timings are largely independent of the material used, and would be similar in time.  This means there's a limit on how much better performance you get by changing the material.  For example when tested on a developer machine, the `momentum_update` step was about three times faster for rubber than sand, but the over all performance improvement was only ten percent.

This scene also shows how to use the `label_sources` option on the `mpm_solver_settings` to split the particles by source geometry so that when meshing the two helices do not merge together.

### Inputs, Controls & Outputs

Two mesh helices are the driver for this example. Any other mesh that can be voxelized could be used instead of the supplied helix. However, the most important thing to consider is the world scale. The scene may need extensive tweaking if the size of the input mesh is drastically different than the helix.

The output of this graph is a mesh ready to be rendered with Arnold. The points from the MPM simulation have been converted into a levelset, then converted to a polygon mesh. The example also includes a `standard_surface_mat` that is wired into an `assign_material` node to define a rendering material for the mesh.

### Best Practices and Tips

The MPM solver does quite a good job at remaining fairly consistent at various resolutions. It is best to work out timing and rough material properties at a preview resolution and slowly increase the resolution to get accurate collisions and more details in the material. While increasing the particles per voxel will give more rubber particle details, there does need to be a small enough detail size to handle self collisions nicely. The `vibration_speed` property on the `source_mpm_rubber` node has a substantial effect on the solver speed. Lower values can greatly help to increase iterations, but at a 'cost'- the resulting simulation will have a very bouncy quality. This can be an acceptable tradeoff when developing the simulation, then increase the `vibration_speed` only as high as it needs to be.

The `file_cache` compound is not required. However, it is strongly recommended to cache out the MPM particles. Do note for efficiency the `split_points` has a `properties` port which defines the particle properties to keep before the `file_cache` compound to reduce the file size as many properties are not required outside of the simulation. It also makes it very easy to iterate on the meshing and render settings without having to worry about losing a simulation result once everything is dialed in. Also, once cached, the rendering could be easily distributed to a render farm if that is available.

_notes.text:
The file_cache is set to passthrough.
When running the simulation at production resolution it is ideal to cache out the simulation data before rendering, as typically the render will take longer than the simulation and can be easily resumed (unlike the simulation)

# polygon Helix

A custom compound for creating a helix in geometry - feel free to take this and use it for your projects!

# MPM Rubber

The MPM rubber material is a simpler material than snow, sand or gel, with purely elastic behavior. 

Resolution is controlled by the *particles_per_voxel* setting.

The behavior of the rubber can be controlled with the *mass_density*, *viscosity*, *volume_preservation* and *vibration speed* settings.

Please check the info tab for in depth explanations of these properties.
The ***ground_plane_influence*** is an influence that does the job of a ground plane for collisions.  You can set the height as well as displaying a representation of the infinite plane.
